map.prompt: A draft makes a single turn around a misplaced coat button. A second follows its owners through six winters. Which form on the course map gives each idea room, and why?
map.answer: Flash can hold one image and a single turn. A long story makes room for a second strand and a real gap in time. These are working conventions: choose by what the material needs.

map.prompt: A narrator spends a page watching a needle fall, then changes from a watcher at the window to the person who dropped it. Which two choices have changed?
map.answer: The time spent on the falling needle is a choice of speed (a stretch). Moving into the second person’s perception changes viewpoint or distance. Slowing a moment does not by itself tell us whose mind we occupy.

map.prompt: Give the first and last line of a flash story about a lost ticket. What promise has the ending answered?
map.answer: One pair: “Every night we checked the empty seat for his ticket.” / “Tonight his ticket was there, folded around ours.” The opening asks about an absence. The last image makes the absence newly personal.
criteria: Make the opening raise a particular question.
Let the last line change how we read a detail from the first.

week-1.prompt: A museum guard wants the last visitor to leave. Write three beats that give the guard a reason to reverse that want. End on a visible action.
week-1.answer: One version: “The guard rattled his keys. The girl held up the photograph from her wallet: the empty plinth with a bronze bird still on it. He turned the entrance sign to CLOSED and drew a chair up for her.” The photograph turns an obstacle into someone worth hearing.
criteria: Establish the guard’s immediate want.
Have an event change the guard’s options.
Let the last action demonstrate the change.

week-1.prompt: Which line compresses time, and which puts us in the room? Point to the smallest piece of evidence for each.

week-1.prompt: Why rewrite the same page with a different material leading each time? What should stay fixed?

week-1.prompt: Plan the 600-word scene due this week. Compress a locksmith’s afternoon into one sentence. Choose the single minute to expand, state the want in five words or fewer, and give the opening and closing actions.
week-1.answer: One plan: “All afternoon people brought her keys for rooms with missing doors.” Expand the minute a little boy brings a door handle instead. Want: “Match the last key.” She starts by pushing the key into his handle. She ends by taking her workshop key from her own pocket and trying that. The handle now connects the problem to her own door.
criteria: Choose an exact minute whose events deserve the space.
Keep the want small enough to act on and give it an obstacle.
Finish with a visible change that the opening made possible.

week-2.prompt: A repairer and a passenger each see a fare-box seal break. Choose a teller for a 600-word revision. Write one sentence only that teller could supply, one fact to withhold, and a short defense of the choice.
week-2.answer: One plan uses the passenger as a witness: “It broke on the third tap; I counted because I knew the conductor would ask.” Withhold whether the repairer had already loosened the seal. criteria: Name one teller and the event both accounts would share.

week-7.prompt: A cook opens a drawer, grabs a towel, touches a cold key. How would ordering by use differ from ordering by weight?

week-12.prompt: A narrator knows an old bridge is closed and gives a traveler the wrong route. A second narrator keeps calling a barricaded bridge “our usual crossing” because accepting its loss would mean selling the house. Distinguish the sources of unreliability.

week-15.prompt: Move from one object in a bakery to the building and then the town in three connected sentences. Make each change of scale alter what the baker can do.
week-15.answer: One version: “The dough stuck to the cold tray. The flat upstairs had drawn the last hot water. Across town the boiler works had locked its gates, so the baker lit the oven and washed the tray in yesterday's tea.” Each enlargement supplies a constraint on the small task.
criteria: Use at least three distinguishable scales.
Connect the scales through an action or consequence.

week-15.prompt: A toll bridge appears in two drafts. In one, two partners meet halfway across it; in the other, one partner sells a ring to pay for the crossing. What job does the setting do in each?
week-15.answer: The first draft mainly uses the bridge as a stage for a meeting. In the second its price puts pressure on an action. If the price also determines who belongs on either bank, the bridge reveals the society too.
criteria: Identify the practical job of place.

week-15.prompt: Invent a local name for a shortcut between a tailor's shop and the bus stop. Make the name reveal a piece of the town's history by changing a present action.
week-15.answer: One version: “Nobody took Tenter Lane with a balloon: the old brass cloth hooks still stood proud of its walls.” The name belongs to a former use, and the object that survives it changes today's route.
criteria: Use a name a local might actually say.

week-15.prompt: A ferry ticket costs twelve dollars. Show the amount from two people's positions in the town. Let payments or objects do the explaining.
week-15.answer: One version: “Lina asked for twelve tickets and signed the slip where the factory's name was printed. Tomas asked whether he could have the twelve back if he walked home.” The same price exposes different kinds of access.
criteria: Use one specific price seen by both people.

week-15.prompt: To study a story built as a walk, what would you put on a map besides street names? Sketch a three-stop example in which the route changes the traveler.
week-15.answer: Record the obstacles in order and what the traveler carries, learns or loses at each one. Example: turnstile (leaves the crate), stairs (returns for the crate), platform (train gone, someone waiting with a trolley). The route produces decisions.
criteria: List an ordered route.
Show a change between the departure and the arrival.

week-15.prompt: Write an out-and-back walk in three sentences. On the return, let one feature of the starting room gain a new meaning.
week-15.answer: One version: “The ticket office clock had stopped at six. I walked the length of the platform and found all the station clocks covered in paper. Back in the office I took my coat off the peg where the clock had thrown its shadow.” The short excursion changes what a dead clock can tell us about the station.
criteria: Complete the return in a consistent tense.
Make the outside observation change the reading of an indoor detail.

week-16.prompt: Open a story with a single impossible fact about a laundry. In the next sentence give an employee a practical consequence to deal with. Keep the delivery matter-of-fact.
week-16.answer: One opening: “The iron pressed the names out of shirts. Edna set a basket beneath the board and began matching the loose letters to the claim tickets.” The second sentence treats the first as a problem with a working routine.
criteria: Introduce one governing impossibility.
Derive a material consequence and keep the tone steady.

week-16.prompt: In A, a woman finds her own handwriting on every label in a house she has never visited; there are ordinary ways this could have happened. In B, evidence keeps both a haunting and a forged diary alive. Which reader experience does each emphasize?
week-16.answer: A makes the familiar feel eerie while staying within possible events, the uncanny. B sustains hesitation between natural and supernatural accounts, the fantastic. An unexplained fact alone would not decide between them.
criteria: Name a defensible mode for each.
Locate the competing explanations or the disturbing familiar detail.

week-16.prompt: In a rented building every door opens onto the floor above. Trace three consequences for the post carrier. Keep the premise unchanged at each step.
week-16.answer: One chain: a parcel marked “2” reaches floor 3, so the carrier sorts the next round one floor early; a ground-floor delivery now needs an entry below street level, so the carrier asks for the cellar key. One physical rule produces the whole chain.
criteria: Follow the original rule at every step.
Let consequences affect a person, an object and a routine.

week-16.prompt: Make a wall calendar feel wrong while everything stays possible. Then add a single observation that requires an impossible fact in the world of your story.
week-16.answer: One pair: “Every square was crossed out, including tomorrow's.” Someone could have done that. “Under the archivist's unbroken gaze, the paper folded yesterday's square over today and halved the length of the day.” The second version changes the world rather than only raising suspicion.
criteria: Distinguish a disturbing but possible observation from a changed physical rule.
Identify the precise detail at which the bargain changes.
week-16.section: Find the threshold in a realist scene

week-16.prompt: A story about a city that has misplaced Tuesday ends with its clerk waking from a dream. Why does that weaken this week's particular exercise? Give one ending that preserves the premise.
week-16.answer: The awakening cancels the premise whose consequences the exercise asks us to trace. One alternative: “The clerk put the two Monday pay packets into separate envelopes. He left Tuesday's drawer open for the morning shift.” The ending resolves a choice and leaves the city's rule intact.
criteria: Explain what accumulated consequence would vanish.
Finish one practical action inside the continuing strange world.

week-16.prompt: A cracked mirror shows one extra visitor in a hotel lobby. Plan two later observations for a story that sustains hesitation between a ghost and an ordinary explanation.
week-16.answer: One pair: a bellhop remembers the extra coat hanging in the lobby before the mirror arrived; the porter finds an old photograph taped to the wall at the exact angle of reflection. One observation feeds each account. Keep track of which facts both accounts can explain.
criteria: Build evidence for two live explanations.
Look for evidence that could unsettle the currently stronger account.

week-17.prompt: Use the same facts—a room fills, one chair stays empty—to make a short build and a short turn. Read both aloud. Where does each place its strongest beat?
week-17.answer: One build: “Coats came in. Coats filled the hooks. Coats spilled onto every chair but his.” One turn: “Every chair was taken. That was what the register said. His held a coat.” The first gathers pressure in a longer third line; the second revises its opening claim.
criteria: Use the same material in both shapes.

week-17.prompt: Besides punctuation, what three features would you measure or listen for when a paragraph feels monotonous? Give one reversible edit for each.
week-17.answer: Measure sentence length, listen for natural stresses, and listen for repeated sounds. Try joining two sentences, moving a stressed word to the end, or replacing one word in an awkward run of similar consonants. Read each change aloud.
criteria: Name length, stress and sound.
Specify an edit whose effect can be heard.

week-17.prompt: A rower watches a race from the bank. Hold two related movements together with a semicolon and let a parenthesis interrupt them with the rower's own thought.
week-17.answer: One version: “Four blades flashed as one; the fifth dragged a thin stripe of light (mine used to do that) all the way to the bend.” The join keeps the crew in motion while the interruption briefly gives us the waiting rower.
criteria: Use the semicolon between related independent clauses.
Let the interruption admit a particular mind and then return to the movement.

week-17.prompt: Write two short sentences about someone giving away a piano. Decide whether to keep them in one paragraph or separate them. Explain what the length of the rest lets the listener do.
week-17.answer: One version: “The movers took the piano at noon. At one, her hand went looking for middle C.” A paragraph break before the second sentence would leave room to hear the missing instrument. In one paragraph the hand's habit follows the removal more quickly.
criteria: Compare the sound aloud both ways.

week-17.prompt: “The slim slick slates slid straight off the cart.” Identify a place your mouth catches. Revise once to preserve a useful sound and once to clear it. Read the two versions aloud.
week-17.answer: One pair: “The slick slates slid off the cart” keeps a sliding hiss. “The wet tiles slipped off the cart” gives more space to the action. Either can work; choose by what the passage asks the listener to notice.
criteria: Name a specific cluster or stress.

week-18.prompt: A clock restorer sets out to prove a tower clock was deliberately stopped. Supply a midpoint discovery that changes the governing question, then an ending that answers the new one.
week-18.answer: One plan: a ledger shows townspeople stopped it together to mark a flood. The question shifts from “Who interfered?” to “Will the restorer restart their memorial?” In the ending she repairs the smaller dial that shows the tides and leaves the hands of the big clock where they are.
criteria: Change the kind of question the reader is asking.
Let the ending make a decision about the revised question.

week-18.prompt: Six witnesses describe a fire. One outline devotes a chapter to each distinct voice; another comes back to the moment a door opened, each time with new evidence. What holds each outline together?
week-18.answer: The first emphasizes chorus, with the voices organizing our attention. The second is a circling return: each revisit changes our understanding of the same instant. A book might combine the two; explain which principle actually determines the chapter order.
criteria: Name both organizing principles.
Give a reason to order the chapters differently under each.

week-18.prompt: Outline one chapter about an apprentice who wants the last shift in a closing print shop. Give the card a want, an obstacle and a change consequential enough for the next card.
week-18.answer: One card: Lea wants to run the farewell edition. The press has been sold and its buyer is at the door. She offers to print the buyer's first order for free if she can run one final sheet afterward. The next card tests what she is willing to print.
criteria: Make the obstacle interfere with this specific want.
Leave the situation measurably different at the break.

week-18.prompt: End a chapter about a missing ledger twice, first with a rest and then with a hook. What question does the rest settle, and what does the hook open?
week-18.answer: One rest: “She laid the ledger back in its square of dust.” Its whereabouts are settled. One hook: “The last entry was dated tomorrow.” Now the reader wants to know who wrote it and why. The incident supports two different demands on attention.
criteria: Close an existing question in one ending.
Open a concrete question grounded in the ledger in the other.

week-18.prompt: A hotel manager prides himself on security. Use an object to give the reader grounds to judge that claim. Compress repeated conduct into one sentence using habitual “would.”
week-18.answer: One version: “The steel safe had a brass plaque screwed over the old letter slot. Each night he would tug the handle twice and leave the screwdrivers on the counter.” The reader can see the weakness while the repeated ritual conveys weeks of confidence.
criteria: Let two material facts imply a judgment.
Use habitual time rather than a single event.

week-18.prompt: How does the lesson distinguish a long story, a novella, linked stories and a novel by the kinds of attention each can carry?
week-18.answer: A long story can develop a second strand and jump across time. A novella can sustain one line of action. In linked stories each piece has its own shape and some person or place carries over. A novel can develop several lines across chapters and extended time. These are working possibilities for planning.
criteria: Give a structural distinction for each form.
Use the distinctions to justify a form for a particular story.

week-18.prompt: A 19,000-word draft sustains one line of action. A classmate says it cannot work as a novella because the length table sets a boundary. How would you use the source note to evaluate the draft?
week-18.answer: The ranges are loose conventions. Check what the sustained line needs: does its question develop across the whole span, and does giving it another strand help or dilute it? The ten architectures are also a working list. The actual pattern of attention gives you evidence for choosing a form.

week-18.prompt: How might a long story handle time or strands, and what rough working length does the lesson give?
week-18.answer: A second strand develops and time can jump substantially. Approximate length: 8,000–20,000 words.

week-18.prompt: How might a novella handle time or strands, and what rough working length does the lesson give?
week-18.answer: One sustained line of action can carry the work without a subplot. Approximate length: 20,000–40,000 words.

week-18.prompt: How might a linked stories handle time or strands, and what rough working length does the lesson give?
week-18.answer: Each story stands on its own while a person or place carries across the book. Approximate length: A book-length collection.

week-18.prompt: How might a novel handle time or strands, and what rough working length does the lesson give?
week-18.answer: Chapters can sustain several lines of action across months or years. Approximate length: Often 50,000 words or more.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Line. One life, in order. Model — Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Double plot. Two stories comment on each other. Model — Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina
week-18.context: Two stories comment on each other.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Day. A single day contains the book. Model — Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway
week-18.context: A single day contains the book.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Year. A round of seasons. Model — Jane Austen, Emma

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Generations. A family and its changes over a century. Model — Thomas Mann, Buddenbrooks
week-18.context: A family and its changes over a century.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Frame. A tale nested in the occasion of its telling. Model — Mary Shelley, Frankenstein
week-18.context: A tale nested in the occasion of its telling.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Chorus. A succession of distinct voices. Model — William Faulkner, As I Lay Dying

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Circling return. The book repeatedly approaches one event. Model — Toni Morrison, Beloved
week-18.context: The book repeatedly approaches one event.

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Linked stories. Separately shaped stories accumulate significance. Model — Jennifer Egan, A Visit from the Goon Squad

week-18.prompt: Which architecture holds a longer work together this way?
week-18.answer: Road. A journey divided into stops. Model — Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

week-18.prompt: What is the job of the opening movement in a long work? What risk should you test for?
week-18.answer: Establish voice, world, and the question. Danger — Extended setup delays the action.

week-18.prompt: What is the job of the middle in a long work? What risk should you test for?
week-18.answer: Change the question at least once. Danger — A succession of similar episodes.

week-18.prompt: What is the job of the set pieces in a long work? What risk should you test for?
week-18.answer: Stage the few scenes a reader will remember. Danger — Bunching them together weakens their force.

week-18.prompt: What is the job of the ending movement in a long work? What risk should you test for?
week-18.answer: Answer the question in its final form. Danger — Answering an early question the book has already left behind.

week-18.prompt: What teller choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Keep an impersonal narrator, without an authorial plea or verdict.

week-18.prompt: What mind choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Use free indirect thought so Emma’s imaginings enter the narrator’s grammar.

week-18.prompt: What time choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Use habitual “would” to let the reader feel the repetition of weeks.

week-18.prompt: What words choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Hunt for the precise noun.

week-18.prompt: What architecture choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Organize three parts around a few widely spaced set pieces.

week-18.prompt: What irony choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Place two facts side by side and let the reader make the judgment.

week-18.prompt: What try it choice would you look for on the Flaubert study card?
week-18.answer: Describe an object closely enough to reveal its owner, then show a repeated action with “would.”

week-18.prompt: Which kind of chapter ending does this line offer?
week-18.answer: Hook. Opens a question.

week-18.prompt: Which kind of chapter ending does this line offer?
week-18.answer: Rest. Closes a question.
week-18.context: At closing time he handed over the keys.

week-18.prompt: Which kind of chapter ending does this line offer?
week-18.answer: Image. Leaves a picture with the reader.
week-18.context: A brass key lay sideways in the white plaster dust.

week-18.prompt: Which kind of chapter ending does this line offer?
week-18.answer: Cut. Interrupts an unfolding scene.
week-18.context: “Then what did you put in the—”

week-18.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of the long form?
week-18.answer: Architecture Try this reading task — Give each chapter one sentence describing its job. Mark the first set piece.

week-18.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of the long form?
week-18.answer: Double plot Try this reading task — Assign chapters to Anna or Levin and find the first point of contact.

week-18.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of the long form?
week-18.answer: Circling return Try this reading task — List each return to the central event and record what additional knowledge it brings.

week-18.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of the long form?
week-18.answer: Novella Try this reading task — Reduce the action to five sentences. Inventory what the book contains beyond plot.

week-19.prompt: A baker wants to open early. A cleaner wants time to finish the floor. Introduce a third corner that changes one person's allegiance. Give each corner a concrete interest.
week-19.answer: One version: a night-shift nurse arrives for the only loaf she can buy before her bus. The cleaner, who rides that bus too, tips up the mop bucket so the baker can reach the counter. Access to the loaf and the bus makes a new alignment possible.
criteria: Show the initial competing wants.
Make the third corner force a visible choice.

week-19.prompt: A cautious apprentice exposes a reckless architect's haste. A former architect now making furniture shows the career the architect once considered. Which is functioning as a foil and which as a double?
week-19.answer: The apprentice is a foil because contrast makes the architect's haste visible. The furniture maker is a double because their life realizes a possible path for the architect. The function comes from the relationship, and can change in another scene.
criteria: Name the relationship that creates each function.
Distinguish contrast in a trait from an alternative life path.

week-19.prompt: Stage a three-person exchange at a counter in three sentences. Establish positions through one witness. Move someone at the point when power changes hands.
week-19.answer: One version: “From the till, Dee could see Rosa at the counter and Min blocking the shop door. ‘We're closed,’ Rosa called. Min held up the deed, and Rosa came around the counter to stand beside Dee.” The counter no longer separates the two employees from each other.
criteria: Locate everyone before the turn.
Keep each detail available to one witness.
Let the movement register a change in relations.

week-19.prompt: Begin with what sounds like a building-wide consensus about who gets the sunny room. End by letting us discover whose opinion it actually is.
week-19.answer: One version: “It was agreed throughout the house that the sunny room was essential to a person who worked with figures, and the treasurer had prudently moved his pillow there already.” The benefit and the pillow identify the source of the general rule.
criteria: Start with a plausible collective judgment.
Use a late detail to disclose a particular interest.

week-19.prompt: A caretaker, a pianist and a child sit at a table. Only one knows the hall has been sold; another believes tonight is an audition. Build a three-person knowledge grid in words and give the third person one question that exposes the mismatch.
week-19.answer: One grid: caretaker knows sale and thinks the others know; pianist knows about the announced audition and assumes the hall will stay open; child sees the chairs being counted. The child asks, “If she's playing here tomorrow, why did he write a price under her stool?”
criteria: List who knows, assumes or merely observes each fact.
Let the question exploit a specific gap in access.
week-19.section: Six drills for the week 18 outline

week-19.prompt: These people both want the last seat. Sketch a different speaking habit for each, then write their two lines without tags so the habits identify them.
week-19.answer: One version: the accountant makes conditions explicit; the usher frames requests as directions. “If I stand until the interval, do I owe the full price?” / “Follow the red carpet. Stop when your knees touch velvet.” The role is audible in what each assumes a sentence should do.
criteria: Keep the want in common.
Distinguish the voices through phrasing or knowledge that belongs to each.

week-19.prompt: Sketch the five-person table scene due this week. Give each person a seat and a different want. Draft the first exchange and give the fifth person a physical move that changes who can act next.
week-19.answer: One plan: At the head the chair wants a signature; opposite, the cook wants the lease renewed. The porter on her right wants his wages; the tenant on her left wants a key; the child by the window wants her mother to stay. “Pass the pen,” the chair says. The child slides the lease under her plate and leaves the pen exactly where it is. Her position and want let her interrupt four adult plans.
criteria: Give each of the five a distinct location and immediate interest.
Make the exchange legible in one point of view.
Use a physical change to alter the balance around the table.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Protagonist. A desire drives the book.
week-19.context: The stage manager wants the first performance to go ahead.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Antagonist. A competing desire obstructs the protagonist.
week-19.context: An inspector wants the theater closed for repairs.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Foil. A contrast brings a particular trait into view.
week-19.context: A meticulous apprentice exposes the manager’s haste.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Confidant. Conversation lets private thought become speech.
week-19.context: The costumer listens before making a suggestion.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Double. Another life shows a path the protagonist might have taken.
week-19.context: A former colleague has left the stage to teach.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Chorus. A group speaks as a collective.
week-19.context: The ushers pass on the same rumor.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Catalyst. Someone arrives, changes the situation, and leaves.
week-19.context: A courier delivers a canceled permit.

week-19.prompt: What cast role could this person or object fill? Explain its function.
week-19.answer: Absent one. We know someone through other people, as in week 5.
week-19.context: The missing owner survives in the staff’s incompatible memories.

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether want makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Can you give each person’s want in five words?

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether speech makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Cover the dialogue tags. Can you tell who speaks?

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether body makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Name one gesture particular to each person.

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether name makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Say the names aloud and check for confusable initials or sounds.

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether knowledge makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Identify what each knows that another person doesn’t.

week-19.prompt: How could you test whether pattern makes the people in a crowded scene distinguishable?
week-19.answer: Find each person’s most revealing opposite.

week-19.prompt: What teller choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Use an ironic, knowledgeable narrator who remains close to a heroine.

week-19.prompt: What mind choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Let free indirect thought involve us in the heroine’s errors.

week-19.prompt: What cast choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Let each member of a small community furnish a different foil.

week-19.prompt: What speech choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Give each participant a recognizable habit of dialogue.

week-19.prompt: What scene choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Assemble the cast for a ball, dinner, or picnic.

week-19.prompt: What sentence choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Keep clauses balanced and place the sting at the end.

week-19.prompt: What shape choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Follow a year, a recognized mistake, and a marriage.

week-19.prompt: What try it choice would you look for on the Austen study card?
week-19.answer: Start with an apparent consensus and gradually disclose whose opinion it is.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: The reader can locate a voice before it speaks.
week-19.context: Place everyone in the opening paragraph.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: The movement identifies the speaker and redirects attention.
week-19.context: Give a new speaker an action when the talk changes hands.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: The entire group stays present without five simultaneous exchanges.
week-19.context: Let two speak while the others do things.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: A shared pronoun can point to several people in the same room.
week-19.context: Use names when pronouns become ambiguous.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: An entrance, exit, or shift of position marks a change.
week-19.context: Move someone at the turning point.

week-19.prompt: When you block a group scene, why use this rule?
week-19.answer: The reader sees the gathering from a continuous vantage point.

week-19.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of cast?
week-19.answer: A group turns upon one cruel remark. Try this reading task — List those present and their positions. Mark the sentence that changes the gathering.
week-19.context: Jane Austen, Emma (1815), Box Hill picnic

week-19.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of cast?
week-19.answer: A full table filtered through one observer. Try this reading task — Sketch the table and give each guest an identifying act of eating or talking.

week-19.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of cast?
week-19.answer: A household introduced rapidly. Try this reading task — List each person with the single detail that fixes them in mind.
week-19.context: Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878), first four chapters

week-19.prompt: What would you mark, count or listen for when reading this work through the lens of cast?
week-19.answer: Six speakers form a chorus. Try this reading task — Give each voice an adjective, then test it against the next thirty pages.
week-19.context: Virginia Woolf, The Waves (1931), first sequence of voices

week-20.prompt: A page repeatedly adds a fragment after a complete sentence. Invent one example, remove the fragment, and describe exactly what disappears. Give the next line a different shape.
week-20.answer: One test: “They cleared the shelves. The high ones too.” Cutting the fragment removes the last place the child hoped her things might survive. Follow with “She fetched the stool anyway and unfolded it beneath the marks in the wallpaper.” The longer action keeps the discovery moving.
criteria: Identify a job a particular fragment performs.
Change the shape of the next sentence and compare the effect.

week-20.prompt: “My voice is cinematic” and “I keep my narrator across the street until the final sentence” are proposed style-card entries. What evidence would make either entry useful, and what single revision could test it?
week-20.answer: Locate a passage, identify the observable choice and name its effect. For the second entry, mark where the reader first gains access to private thought; move that moment to the first sentence and compare the suspense. The broader label needs comparable evidence from the page.
criteria: Identify an actual feature a second reader could locate.
Change one feature and specify what effect to compare.

week-20.prompt: Describe a failed audition in first person without the word “I.” Then lift the rule for one sentence. What did the constraint make you notice?
week-20.answer: One version: “My name was still chalked on the board when the next violin started.” With the rule lifted: “I took the chalk home in my pocket.” The first sentence borrows the narrator's eyes; the second earns the pronoun through an action the narrator chooses.
criteria: Follow the drafting rule literally.
Name one discovery worth keeping after lifting it.

week-20.prompt: Outline a second strand for a story about a vanished shop sign. Include a time gap, a changed governing question and a final return of one object. Let both strands matter to the ending.
week-20.answer: One outline: a child saves a cracked enamel letter when the shop closes. Twenty years later an archivist traces the sign and discovers the shop was shared by three families. “Where did it go?” becomes “Whose name goes beneath it?” In the last scene the child, now a sign painter, sets the old letter between three new names.
criteria: Give the second strand a distinct time or place.
Make the final choice depend on both strands.
Return a motif with a changed significance.

week-20.prompt: After the earlier revision checks, what two tests does the final lesson add? What evidence could another reader give you for each?
week-20.answer: Ask whether the reader can trace a motif from its first use through transformation and recognize this story's author from an earlier work. Ask for the motif's first and final appearances, then for a recurring sentence or narrative choice and an example from each story.
criteria: Separate pattern within one work from a signature across works.
Ask for textual evidence for each.

week-20.prompt: Choose one week-11-to-19 move and design a ten-minute transfer exercise for tomorrow. Decide what you will compare when you revisit the work.
week-20.answer: One exercise: take yesterday's argument and retell it through a second witness who uses one revealing aside. Tomorrow compare the two versions with names covered and mark the first words that give each witness away. Save a line of evidence for a later style card.
criteria: Specify an observed craft move.
Name the fresh passage or situation in which to use it.
Choose a concrete comparison you can repeat.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under teller? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Who speaks, in which person and tense? One experiment — Try a close third-person version of a first-person scene.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under distance? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Where does the narration sit on the distance scale? One experiment — Pull back from close interior narration once on a page.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under mind? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: How does thought move or revise itself? One experiment — Keep an audible self-correction or trace a different thought pattern.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under time? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: How much story time passes? Where does memory enter? One experiment — Add a second clock.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under people? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Who speaks and who is only recalled? One experiment — Give a second person a line of speech.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under world? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: What sounds, sights, and objects can you recover? One experiment — Name three specific things you omitted.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under sentence? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: How do statements, fragments, and long sentences alternate? One experiment — Try one sustained sentence on a page of short ones.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under diction? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Where do you use familiar or invented words? One experiment — Keep a plain passage and try a single necessary coinage.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under figure? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: How many images recur or extend across the page? One experiment — Develop one sustained comparison.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under tone? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Which two adjectives describe the voice? What earns them? One experiment — Retain the tone through a different event.

week-20.prompt: On a personal style card, what evidence would you record under ending? Suggest a change to test that habit.
week-20.answer: Do you leave an image, question, answer, or action? One experiment — Write a second ending and compare its effect.

week-20.prompt: Which recurring move can you identify here? Describe its job and the risk of overusing it.
week-20.answer: Fragment after a statement. Points to the detail that matters. Becomes predictable if every paragraph uses it.
week-20.context: “They took the scenery. Even the moon.”

week-20.prompt: Which recurring move can you identify here? Describe its job and the risk of overusing it.
week-20.answer: Self-correction. Lets a thought change within the sentence. Can sound coy.

week-20.prompt: Which recurring move can you identify here? Describe its job and the risk of overusing it.
week-20.answer: Coinage. Names an effect in a particular voice. Several coinages together can distract.

week-20.prompt: Which recurring move can you identify here? Describe its job and the risk of overusing it.
week-20.answer: Spoken or off-register word. Retains the texture of a speaking voice. Can become imprecise.

week-20.prompt: Which recurring move can you identify here? Describe its job and the risk of overusing it.
week-20.answer: Shrug of uncertainty. Leaves an ambiguity alive. A narrator who always shrugs may never discover anything.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Vladimir Nabokov study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: The aside.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Anton Chekhov study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A small fact beside an understated large feeling.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the James Joyce study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: An object named three times to make an echo.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Leo Tolstoy study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A body placed exactly in space.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the William Faulkner study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A proper noun and a place with a past.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Franz Kafka study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A flat statement of the impossible.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Virginia Woolf study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A semicolon and a parenthetical interruption.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Gustave Flaubert study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: Habitual “would” and an object that judges its owner.

week-20.prompt: Which craft move from the Jane Austen study could you borrow and test on a new page?
week-20.answer: A general truth that contracts into one person’s opinion.

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Choose nouns and verbs precisely.

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Hear strong beats and short, often Germanic words.

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Show the scene through what the narrator observes.

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Build a voice from doubt.

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Compress and use the space between sentences.
week-20.context: Cap every sentence at ten words

week-20.prompt: What does this temporary drafting constraint make you practise?
week-20.answer: Test how much weight the syntax can carry.
week-20.context: Fill a page with one sentence

week-20.prompt: How would you test this rule for keeping a signature move?
week-20.answer: Remove it and name exactly what disappears.

week-20.prompt: How would you test this rule for keeping a signature move?
week-20.answer: Try using it at most once on a page and count the instances.

week-20.prompt: How would you test this rule for keeping a signature move?
week-20.answer: Change the shape of a second fragment or interruption.

week-20.prompt: How would you test this rule for keeping a signature move?
week-20.answer: Answer a characteristic fragment with a sustained sentence.

week-20.prompt: How would you test this rule for keeping a signature move?
week-20.answer: Omit one signature for an entire story and see what takes its place.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the opening and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Establish voice, want, world, and one signature. Revisit — Weeks 11 and 15 Working length: 1,000 words.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the first strand and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Use scenes with another person and an unspoken issue. Revisit — Weeks 12 and 19 Working length: 1,500 words.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the second strand and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Enter another time or place and plant a motif. Revisit — Weeks 13 and 18 Working length: 1,500 words.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the turn and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Change the governing question and introduce strangeness if the story uses it. Revisit — Week 16 Working length: 1,200 words.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the body and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Convey the hardest feeling through observable detail. Revisit — Week 14 Working length: 1,300 words.

week-20.prompt: In the capstone plan, what belongs in the ending and what earlier work could guide it?
week-20.answer: Bring the strands together, return the motif changed, and score the final paragraph. Revisit — Weeks 13 and 17 Working length: 1,500 words.

week-20.prompt: What does the course propose doing daily after week twenty?
week-20.answer: Transpose a page you wrote yesterday along one craft axis.

week-20.prompt: What does the course propose doing weekly after week twenty?
week-20.answer: Take apart one story from the Map’s reading shelf with a pencil.

week-20.prompt: What does the course propose doing monthly after week twenty?
week-20.answer: Apprentice yourself to another writer. Copy a page by hand, make an author card, and write a short exercise using one observed technique.

week-20.prompt: What does the course propose doing every ten weeks after week twenty?
week-20.answer: Finish a story.

week-20.prompt: What does the course propose doing yearly after week twenty?
week-20.answer: Return to the page you began with and write a fresh style card for it.
